gloss_terse: To rebuke sharply, reprove with authority; used of human correction and divine censure of nations, the sea, and evil.
gloss_readable: A verb expressing forceful verbal reproof, ranging from a father scolding his son (Gen 37:10) to God rebuking the nations and the cosmic waters. When Jacob rebukes Joseph, the word carries familial authority; when God rebukes the Red Sea (Ps 106:9) or Satan (Zech 3:2), it conveys sovereign command that reshapes reality. Remarkably, all six translation languages render every occurrence with a single equivalent — English 'rebuke,' Spanish 'reprender' — confirming its tight semantic unity across all 14 uses.

senses.1: To sharply reprimand or censure, expressing strong disapproval or authoritative correction. Covers both human rebuke — a father chiding his son (Gen 37:10), reapers warned not to harass Ruth (Ruth 2:16) — and divine rebuke where God's word carries cosmic force, stilling seas (Ps 106:9, Nah 1:4) and silencing the accuser (Zech 3:2). The uniform rendering across English, Spanish, French, and German confirms a single cohesive sense without semantic drift.

gloss_terse: Gershom — personal name meaning 'sojourner there,' borne by Moses' firstborn and several Levites.
gloss_readable: A proper masculine name explained by popular etymology as 'a stranger there' (from גֵּר שָׁם), first given by Moses to his firstborn son in Midian because 'I have been a sojourner in a foreign land' (Exod 2:22). The name reappears for a Levitical ancestor (1 Chr 6:16–17, often interchangeable with Gershon) and a descendant of Phinehas who returned with Ezra (Ezra 8:2). Spanish renders it 'Guersom/Gershom,' French varies between 'Guerschom' and 'Gershom,' reflecting the guttural and sibilant challenges this name poses across languages.

senses.1: The Hebrew personal name Gershom (גֵּרְשֹׁם), etymologically linked to גּוּר ('to sojourn'). Primarily identifies Moses' firstborn (Exod 2:22, 18:3; Judg 18:30), but also a Levitical lineage head sometimes written Gershon (1 Chr 6:16–17; 15:7; 23:15–16; 26:24) and a returnee ancestor under Ezra (Ezra 8:2). The slight spelling variation between גֵּרְשֹׁם and גֵּרְשׁוֹם across manuscripts reflects standard orthographic fluidity in proper names.

gloss_terse: A tribal banner or military standard marking Israelite camp divisions and marching order in the wilderness.
gloss_readable: Refers to the large standards carried by each of the four three-tribe divisions during Israel's wilderness encampment and march. Nearly all 14 occurrences appear in Numbers 1–2 and 10, where each דֶּגֶל heads a camp of three tribes — Judah to the east, Reuben to the south, Ephraim to the west, Dan to the north. The single figurative use in Song of Solomon 2:4, 'his banner over me is love,' transforms the military emblem into an intimate image of covenantal protection. Spanish consistently uses 'bandera,' while English alternates between 'banner' and 'standard.'

senses.1: A military or tribal standard (banner, flag) designating the four major divisions of the Israelite encampment in the wilderness. Used almost exclusively in Numbers (1:52; 2:2–34; 10:14–25) to describe the organized arrangement of tribes around the tabernacle, each division rallying under its own דֶּגֶל alongside its tribal signs (אֹתֹת). The lone figurative appearance in Song of Solomon 2:4 — 'his banner over me is love' — poetically recasts the military emblem as a canopy of beloved protection.

gloss_terse: Zimri — a Hebrew personal name borne by a Simeonite prince, a king of Israel, and Judahite and Benjamite figures.
gloss_readable: A proper masculine name identifying at least four individuals in the Hebrew Bible. Most prominent is the Israelite king who assassinated Elah and reigned just seven days before Omri's siege drove him to self-immolation (1 Kgs 16:9–20); Jezebel's taunt 'Is it peace, Zimri?' (2 Kgs 9:31) preserves his infamy as a regicide. The name also belongs to the Simeonite prince slain by Phinehas at Baal-peor (Num 25:14), a grandson of Judah (1 Chr 2:6), and a Benjamite descendant of Saul (1 Chr 8:36; 9:42).

senses.1: The proper name Zimri (זִמְרִי), borne by multiple Old Testament figures: (a) a Simeonite prince killed by Phinehas for bringing a Midianite woman into the Israelite camp (Num 25:14); (b) the fifth king of Israel's northern kingdom, who murdered Elah and reigned only seven days before burning the palace over himself (1 Kgs 16:9–18); (c) a grandson of Zerah of Judah (1 Chr 2:6); and (d) a Benjamite in Saul's genealogy (1 Chr 8:36; 9:42). The Septuagint renders it Ζαμβρί throughout.

gloss_terse: Hushai — personal name of David's trusted counselor, 'the Archite,' who thwarted Absalom's revolt.
gloss_readable: A proper name identifying Hushai the Archite, one of David's most loyal advisors, designated his 'friend' (רֵעֶה דָוִד). During Absalom's rebellion, David sent Hushai back to Jerusalem to counter Ahithophel's counsel — a stratagem that proved decisive when Hushai persuaded Absalom to delay his pursuit, buying David time to escape across the Jordan (2 Sam 15:32–17:16). His son Baana later served as one of Solomon's district officers (1 Kgs 4:16). French and German transliterate the name as 'Huschai,' while Spanish renders it 'Jusai/Jushai.'

senses.1: The Hebrew personal name Hushai (חוּשַׁי), identifying primarily Hushai the Archite, David's confidant and counselor who played a pivotal role in Absalom's rebellion by undermining Ahithophel's shrewd military advice (2 Sam 15:32–17:16). Called 'David's friend' (רֵעֶה דָוִד), a title that may designate a formal court position. Also referenced as the father of Baana, one of Solomon's twelve district governors (1 Kgs 4:16). The name appears in 1 Chronicles 27:33 confirming his role alongside Ahithophel.

gloss_terse: A seal or signet-ring used for authenticating documents, marking ownership, and as a figure of preciousness.
gloss_readable: Denotes both the physical seal-stone and the signet ring worn on the hand or hung from a cord around the neck. Judah pledges his seal-cord to Tamar as surety (Gen 38:18), Jezebel stamps Naboth's death warrant with Ahab's seal (1 Kgs 21:8), and the priestly vestments are engraved 'like the engravings of a seal' (Exod 28:11, 21, 36). In prophetic speech, Haggai likens Zerubbabel to God's signet ring (Hag 2:23), and Song of Solomon 8:6 pleads, 'Set me as a seal upon your heart.' Spanish distinguishes 'sello' (seal) from 'anillo de sellar' (signet ring), while German uses 'Siegel.'

senses.1: A seal or signet-ring (חוֹתָם / חֹתָם) — a personal object of authentication and authority. Physically, it could be hung from a cord about the neck (Gen 38:18) or worn on the right hand (Jer 22:24). Its uses span the practical — stamping royal documents (1 Kgs 21:8) and engraving priestly stones with the technique described as 'engravings of a seal' (Exod 28:11, 39:6) — and the figurative, where God declares Zerubbabel his signet (Hag 2:23) and the beloved asks to be set as a seal upon the heart (Song 8:6). Its preciousness makes it apt metaphor for what is uniquely treasured.

gloss_terse: Wise men, sages — Aramaic term for the learned class at the Babylonian court possessing esoteric knowledge.
gloss_readable: An Aramaic noun (חַכִּים) occurring exclusively in Daniel, designating the professional class of wise men or sages at the Babylonian and Persian courts. These חַכִּימִין appear alongside magicians, enchanters, and astrologers as court advisors whom Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar consult for dream interpretation and reading cryptic signs. When God reveals Nebuchadnezzar's dream to Daniel, it is said that God 'gives wisdom to the wise' (Dan 2:21), using the same root. English and Spanish render the term straightforwardly as 'wise men' and 'sabios,' while French and German leave several occurrences untranslated.

senses.1: Aramaic plural noun referring to the professional class of wise men (sages) at the Babylonian and Persian royal courts, who possessed esoteric learning and served as royal counselors alongside magicians and astrologers (Dan 2:12–14, 18, 24, 27; 4:3; 5:7–8, 15). Nebuchadnezzar's decree to destroy all wise men of Babylon (Dan 2:12–13) and Daniel's subsequent vindication among them form the dramatic core. The singular-abstract use in Daniel 2:21, 'He gives wisdom to the wise,' plays on the root to affirm divine sovereignty over all human sagacity.

gloss_terse: A perforated cake or ring-shaped bread used in Israelite grain offerings and ritual meals.
gloss_readable: A feminine noun denoting a specific type of baked offering — likely a perforated or ring-shaped cake, as the name may derive from the root meaning 'to pierce.' All 14 occurrences appear in ritual contexts within the Pentateuch. These cakes are prepared variously: unleavened and mixed with oil for the grain offering (Lev 2:4; 7:12), baked from fine flour for the bread of the Presence (Lev 24:5), offered as firstfruits from dough (Num 15:20), or included in the consecration of priests (Exod 29:2, 23; Lev 8:26). Spanish uses 'torta' throughout, while English consistently renders it 'cake.'

senses.1: A type of cake or bread, probably perforated or ring-shaped (from the root חלל, 'to bore, pierce'), prepared exclusively for sacrificial and ritual use. Varieties include: unleavened cakes mixed with oil for the grain offering (Lev 2:4; 7:12), fine-flour cakes for the bread of the Presence (Lev 24:5), firstfruit dough offerings (Num 15:20), and priestly consecration bread (Exod 29:2, 23; Lev 8:26). Also distributed to the people during David's celebration when the ark was brought to Jerusalem (2 Sam 6:19). The term is confined to Priestly and related texts.

gloss_terse: Heth — eponymous ancestor of the Hittites, listed as a son of Canaan in the Table of Nations.
gloss_readable: A proper masculine name identifying the ancestor-figure of the Hittites (בְּנֵי חֵת, 'sons of Heth'). In the Table of Nations, Heth is listed as Canaan's son (Gen 10:15; 1 Chr 1:13). The name appears most frequently in the phrase 'sons of Heth,' denoting the local population at Hebron from whom Abraham purchased the cave of Machpelah as a burial site (Gen 23:3–20; 25:10; 49:32). The 'daughters of Heth' are Esau's Hittite wives, a source of grief to Rebekah (Gen 27:46). French and German transliterate as 'Heth' and 'Chet' respectively.

senses.1: The proper name Heth (חֵת), the eponymous ancestor of the Hittites, presented as a son of Canaan (Gen 10:15; 1 Chr 1:13). Almost all occurrences use the construct 'sons of Heth' (בְּנֵי חֵת) to designate the Hittite population resident at Hebron in the patriarchal period, particularly in the Machpelah purchase narrative (Gen 23:3–20; 25:10; 49:32). The phrase 'daughters of Heth' (בְּנוֹת חֵת) in Gen 27:46 identifies the Hittite women Esau married. Etymology and precise meaning of the name remain uncertain.

gloss_terse: Dry land or dry ground, especially as a path through parted waters or as earth distinct from sea.
gloss_readable: A feminine noun meaning dry ground, used in vivid contrast with water throughout the Old Testament. At creation, God commands the waters to gather so that the יַבָּשָׁה appears (Gen 1:9–10). The word reaches its dramatic peak in the exodus: Israel crosses the Red Sea on dry ground (Exod 14:16, 22, 29; 15:19) and later the Jordan (Josh 4:22). Jonah confesses that the Lord made both sea and dry land (Jon 1:9), and the great fish vomits him onto the יַבָּשָׁה (Jon 2:10). Isaiah uses it figuratively for a parched Israel that God will refresh with his Spirit (Isa 44:3).

senses.1: Dry ground or dry land (יַבָּשָׁה), used in opposition to water or sea. Appears in three major thematic clusters: (a) creation, where dry land emerges from gathered waters (Gen 1:9–10); (b) salvation-through-water narratives, where God provides a dry path through the Red Sea (Exod 14:16, 22, 29; 15:19; Neh 9:11; Ps 66:6) and the Jordan (Josh 4:22); and (c) Jonah's story, where the prophet acknowledges God as maker of sea and dry land (Jon 1:9) and is delivered onto shore (Jon 2:10). Isaiah 44:3 uses it figuratively of spiritual barrenness that God will revive.
